questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.syllabus_ref: C.4 Standing waves and resonance, with C.2 Wave model
questions.subtopic: C.4 Two determinations of the same speed by standing waves in a tube, where the neglected end correction is worth more than either measurement's uncertainty
questions.challenge_mechanism: The two students measure the same quantity and disagree by twelve parts in a thousand, and the disagreement is not noise. Student B drives a tube of fixed length and takes the resonant frequency to give $v = 4fL$; the true relation is $v = 4f(L + e)$ with $e$ about $5.5\ \mathrm{mm}$, and leaving $e$ out costs exactly the difference observed. The uncertainty analysis is a decoy: neither student's random uncertainties come close to explaining a discrepancy that is entirely systematic and entirely predictable.

stimulus.title: Two students measure the speed of sound in air
stimulus.body: Student A held a loudspeaker driven by a tuning fork marked $512\ \mathrm{Hz}$ over the open end of a tube of variable length and moved the tube's water level until he heard the note become loud. He recorded the position of the tube's open upper end at the first three resonances, reading the metre rule to the nearest $\pm 1\ \mathrm{mm}$. Student B used a tube of fixed length $0.500 \pm 0.001\ \mathrm{m}$ and a signal generator connected to a loudspeaker held against the open end; he raised and lowered the frequency until the note became loud and recorded the frequency each time. The generator scale has a resolution of $1\ \mathrm{Hz}$. He recorded successive resonances at $169\ \mathrm{Hz}$, $510\ \mathrm{Hz}$ and $843\ \mathrm{Hz}$. Both experiments were done at the same time and the air temperature was $19.0\ \mathrm{^{\circ}C}$, which both students took to be $20\ \mathrm{^{\circ}C}$. The internal diameter of both tubes was $36\ \mathrm{mm}$.

table.caption: Student A: positions of the first three resonances

questions.question: The two determinations of the speed of sound, and the readings each student took, are described in the stimulus and its table. Answer all parts using those readings.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the wavelength of the sound in Student A's tube from the spacing of his three resonance positions, and hence calculate his value for the speed of sound.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the end correction of the tube from Student A's first resonance position, and explain why the spacing of the positions cannot give it.

parts.label: c
parts.text: One of Student B's three frequencies is inconsistent with the others. Identify it, justify your choice, determine Student B's value for the speed of sound from the remaining two readings, and explain why his value is systematically lower than Student A's.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Evaluate which of the two determinations of the speed of sound should be quoted, comparing the effect of random uncertainty on each with the effect of the systematic term.

questions.answer:
**(a)** Successive resonances in a tube closed at one end occur at $L = \dfrac{\lambda}{4} - e$, $\dfrac{3\lambda}{4} - e$, $\dfrac{5\lambda}{4} - e$, so consecutive positions differ by $\dfrac{\lambda}{2}$ (M1).

$$0.494 - 0.161 = 0.333\ \mathrm{m}, \qquad 0.827 - 0.494 = 0.333\ \mathrm{m} \;\; (A1).$$
$$\lambda = 2 \times 0.333 = 0.666\ \mathrm{m}, \qquad v = f\lambda = 512 \times 0.666 = 341\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}} \;\; (A1).$$
To three significant figures, $v = 341\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The two spacings agree to the nearest millimetre, so the random uncertainty on $\lambda$ is about $\dfrac{0.002}{0.333} = 0.6\%$ at worst, and on $v$ it is smaller still.

**(b)** The first resonance occurs where $L + e = \dfrac{\lambda}{4}$ (M1), so
$$e = \frac{\lambda}{4} - L_{1} = 0.1665 - 0.161 = 0.0055\ \mathrm{m} = 5.5\ \mathrm{mm} \;\; (A1).$$

The spacing cannot give it because $e$ is common to every resonance position. Subtracting one position from the next removes $e$ entirely: $L_{2} - L_{1} = \dfrac{\lambda}{2}$ whatever the end correction is. The spacing therefore determines $\lambda$ but carries no information about $e$, and it is only by referring a position to the *beginning* of the pattern -- which requires knowing that the first resonance is a quarter wavelength -- that $e$ can be extracted. For this tube the correction is $5.5\ \mathrm{mm}$, which is about $0.3$ of the $18\ \mathrm{mm}$ radius, as expected for a tube of this diameter.

**(c)** Two of the three frequencies should differ by twice the fundamental. Using the first and third,
$$\frac{843 - 169}{4} = \frac{674}{4} = 168.5\ \mathrm{Hz} \;\; (M1),$$
so the middle resonance should be at $169 + 2(168.5) = 506\ \mathrm{Hz}$, and $510\ \mathrm{Hz}$ is the inconsistent reading (A1). A $4\ \mathrm{Hz}$ error is four times the generator's $1\ \mathrm{Hz}$ resolution.

Student B used $v = 4f_{0}L$ with the first resonance at the fundamental:
$$v = 4 \times 168.5 \times 0.500 = 337\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}} \;\; (A1).$$

His value is lower by $341 - 337 = 4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, which is $1.2\%$. The cause is that he omitted the end correction. The correct relation is $v = 4f_{0}(L + e)$, so
$$v = 4 \times 168.5 \times (0.500 + 0.0055) = 341\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}},$$
which is Student A's value to three significant figures. Omitting $e$ is not a random error: it always makes the effective length too short, so the inferred speed is always too low, and the size of the effect is fixed by the tube rather than by the care taken in reading the dial. The anomaly at $510\ \mathrm{Hz}$ is a separate matter -- probably the reading was taken while the generator's display was still settling -- and it does not affect the value used, because the fundamental was obtained from the first and third readings.

**(d)** Student A's value should be quoted (A1).

His random uncertainty is dominated by the $\pm 1\ \mathrm{mm}$ reading of the positions, which over a $333\ \mathrm{mm}$ spacing is $0.3\%$, and the tuning fork's frequency is a specification held to better than $0.1\%$. His systematic term is handled rather than ignored: the end correction is obtained from the data and applied, so what remains is the assumption that $e$ is the same at every resonance, which is good to well under a millimetre.

Student B's random uncertainties are comparable -- $1\ \mathrm{Hz}$ in $169\ \mathrm{Hz}$ is $0.6\%$ -- but he carries an unaddressed systematic term of $1.1\%$ from the omitted end correction, and a systematic term is not reduced by repeating the measurement. His result is therefore both lower than Student A's and less trustworthy, and the fact that correcting $e$ brings his value onto Student A's is itself evidence that the correction is the right explanation rather than an arbitrary adjustment (A1).
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) (M1) for recognising that consecutive resonance positions differ by half a wavelength, (A1) for $\lambda = 0.666\ \mathrm{m}$, (A1) for $v = 341\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ with unit. A candidate who divides the full span by two instead of by four -- using $0.827 - 0.161$ as a single wavelength -- obtains $0.333\ \mathrm{m}$ and cannot score the last two marks.

(b) (M1) for the relation $L_{1} + e = \lambda/4$, (A1) for $5.5\ \mathrm{mm}$. The explanation is required for the second mark: a bare number with no statement about why the spacing is blind to $e$ scores (M1) only. Accept $5$ or $6\ \mathrm{mm}$ from a candidate who rounds $\lambda/4$ first; the argument is what is being marked.

(c) (M1) for using the first and third readings to obtain the spacing, (A1) for identifying $510\ \mathrm{Hz}$, (A1) for a value of $v$ determined from the remaining readings. A candidate who identifies the anomaly but then uses all three readings -- averaging, or fitting through all three -- forfeits the third mark; the question asks for the value from the remaining two. The explanation of the direction of the discrepancy is required somewhere in the response for full credit; a value of $337\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ with no comment about the end correction scores the three marks but the candidate should be reminded of the cause.

(d) (A1) for choosing Student A, (A1) for the comparison involving both a random and a systematic term. "Student A is more accurate" alone scores the first mark only; the comparison must reach the point that a systematic term is not reduced by repetition, or the equivalent statement that the discrepancy in (c) is predicted rather than observed.

Condonation: $v = 340\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ is accepted in (a) from a candidate who uses the accepted value of the speed of sound as a check; the calculated value must appear. Follow-through: a candidate whose $f_{0}$ in (c) is obtained from the first and third readings but whose arithmetic is wrong is credited the (M1) and, if the anomaly is correctly named, the (A1); the value mark follows their own $f_{0}$.

Forfeits: treating the $510\ \mathrm{Hz}$ reading as a random error to be averaged out, which removes the anomaly without explaining it; and quoting a percentage uncertainty from the three readings without noticing that the discrepancy between the two students is systematic.
questions.explanation:
Two students measure one number and get $341$ and $337$. The reflex is to ask which is careless, and the answer here is neither. The gap is $1.2\%$, and every random uncertainty in the experiment is smaller than that: the positions are read to a millimetre over a third of a metre, and the frequencies to a hertz in a hundred and seventy. Something systematic is at work, and the item is built so that it can be identified rather than guessed at.

The systematic term is the end correction. A tube closed at one end has an antinode slightly outside the open end, so the acoustically effective length is $L + e$ with $e$ roughly a third of the radius -- here $5.5\ \mathrm{mm}$ for an $18\ \mathrm{mm}$ radius. Student A's method extracts it because he refers an absolute position to the quarter-wavelength condition. Student B's method cannot, because he never uses a position at all: he treats the tube length as the whole of the acoustically effective length and computes $4fL$. The error is one-sided and always in the same direction, and $4fL$ with $f = 168.5\ \mathrm{Hz}$ gives $337$ against the $341$ that $4f(L+e)$ gives. The agreement after correction is the point of part (d): a candidate who finds the removal of $e$ turning $337$ into $341$ has located the cause, not merely adjusted a number.

The seeded anomaly is a different lesson. The three frequencies $169$, $510$ and $843$ should be equally spaced in steps of twice the fundamental, and $169$ to $843$ is four steps of $168.5$, which puts the middle reading at $506$ and not $510$. The reading is $4\ \mathrm{Hz}$ out -- four times the dial's resolution -- and the correct response is to identify it, exclude it and say what probably happened. Averaging the three frequencies to "fix" the anomaly is the classic wrong turn, because the average of a consistent pair and an inconsistent third is inconsistent with all three.

The two lessons are connected and it is worth saying how. A discrepancy that is larger than the uncertainties and always in the same direction is a systematic effect and needs a mechanism; a single reading that violates a pattern the others obey is an anomaly and needs to be excluded. Confusing the two -- treating the systematic offset as noise, or treating the anomaly as a discovery -- produces either a wrong answer or a wrong explanation, and the question is arranged so that both mistakes are available.

provenance.adaptation: Original. Resonance-tube determinations of the speed of sound are a standard practical in every syllabus; what is written here is the comparison of a position-based and a frequency-based method on the same tube, arranged so that the end correction is the whole of the discrepancy and neither student's random uncertainty can account for it.

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Take both students' values at face value, compute an average or a percentage difference, and explain the disagreement of about one per cent by citing the reading uncertainties, since one millimetre in a third of a metre and one hertz in a hundred and seventy sound large enough to cover it.
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: The two determinations differ by a systematic term the uncertainty budget cannot reach, because the fixed-length method computes four f L where the acoustically effective length is L plus an end correction of about five and a half millimetres, which lowers the inferred speed by one point one per cent in one direction only.
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: The discrepancy is attributed to random error and the two values are averaged into a single answer near three hundred and thirty nine metres per second, with the end correction either not computed or computed and then not connected to the difference between the two methods.

verification.method: The wavelength, the end correction and both speeds were recomputed from the tabulated positions and frequencies. The end correction was checked for consistency with the tube diameter (e = 0.3 x radius is the standard expectation for a flanged tube of this kind). The anomalous frequency was located by forming the spacing from the first and third readings and predicting the middle one, and the corrected value was confirmed to reproduce Student A's speed to the significant figures quoted. The change in v from omitting e was evaluated as a ratio: 0.500/0.5055 = 0.9891, giving 337.3 from 341.
solution_skeleton: take the differences of the resonance positions as successive half wavelengths
refer the first resonance to the quarter wavelength condition to extract the end correction
form the spacing of the frequency readings and predict the reading that breaks the pattern
apply the end correction to the fixed length method and compare the two speeds
separate the systematic discrepancy from the random uncertainties and rank the two methods

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.syllabus_ref: A.2 Forces and momentum, with A.1 Kinematics
questions.topic: Theme A: Space, time and motion
questions.subtopic: A.2 An impulse obtained as the area under a force-time record whose sampling interval changed part-way through, so that the area depends on reading the time column rather than assuming a constant step
questions.challenge_mechanism: The impulse is an area and the area is not hard, but the record was taken by a logger on an automatic rate and the time column steps by $10\ \mathrm{ms}$, then $5\ \mathrm{ms}$, then $10\ \mathrm{ms}$ again. A candidate who assumes a uniform step multiplies a mean force by a duration that the data does not have, and the error is $29\%$ in the impulse and $18\%$ in the final speed. The trap needs no physics at all, only the discipline of using the abscissa actually given.

stimulus.title: A collision recorded by a force sensor
stimulus.body: A trolley of mass $0.850 \pm 0.001\ \mathrm{kg}$ was pushed towards a force sensor mounted on the end of a track and bounced off it. A light gate placed just before the sensor measured the trolley's speed before the collision as $0.450 \pm 0.005\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The sensor's output was logged, and the logger was left on its automatic sampling setting. The record begins when the trolley first touched the sensor. The manufacturer states a force resolution of $\pm 0.2\ \mathrm{N}$ and a timing uncertainty of $\pm 0.2\ \mathrm{ms}$ on each sample; the logger's activity log shows that its sampling interval changed during the record. No uncertainty is quoted for the impact duration itself.

questions.question: The force sensor's record of the collision, the trolley's mass and the light gate's reading of the approach speed are given in the stimulus and its table. Answer all parts using those readings.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the two different sampling intervals present in the record and the number of intervals of each kind, and explain why a trapezium rule applied to this table must use the time differences as given.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the impulse delivered to the trolley, using the trapezium rule on the recorded pairs of values and stating the unit of your answer.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine the trolley's speed immediately after the collision, and determine the value a candidate who assumed a constant $10\ \mathrm{ms}$ interval would obtain for the impulse and for that speed.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest what should have been recorded at the time to make this record analysable without ambiguity, and state how the uncertainty in the impulse could best be estimated from the data available.

questions.answer:
**(a)** Reading the time column: the first four intervals are $10\ \mathrm{ms}$ each, the intervals $30 \to 35 \to 40$ are $5\ \mathrm{ms}$ each, and the last two are $10\ \mathrm{ms}$ (A1). So there are **four** intervals of $10\ \mathrm{ms}$ ($0$-$10$, $10$-$20$, $20$-$30$, $40$-$50$, $50$-$60$ is five) -- counting them explicitly: $0$-$10$, $10$-$20$, $20$-$30$, $40$-$50$ and $50$-$60$ are five intervals of $10\ \mathrm{ms}$, and $30$-$35$, $35$-$40$ are two intervals of $5\ \mathrm{ms}$ (A1). Total record length $60\ \mathrm{ms}$.

The trapezium rule approximates $\int F\,dt$ by $\sum \tfrac{1}{2}(F_{i} + F_{i+1})\Delta t_{i}$, so each pair of forces must be weighted by the time difference that actually separates them. The force is not a function of sample number; it is a function of time, and the samples are not equally spaced in time. Using a single step $\Delta t = 10\ \mathrm{ms}$ for all seven intervals would assign the same weight to a $5\ \mathrm{ms}$ interval as to a $10\ \mathrm{ms}$ one, which inflates the area near the peak where the sampling was fastest.

**(b)** Apply the trapezium rule interval by interval (M1):
$$\begin{aligned}
0\text{-}10: &\ \tfrac{1}{2}(0.0 + 4.2)(10) = 21.0 \\
10\text{-}20: &\ \tfrac{1}{2}(4.2 + 9.8)(10) = 70.0 \\
20\text{-}30: &\ \tfrac{1}{2}(9.8 + 15.6)(10) = 127.0 \\
30\text{-}35: &\ \tfrac{1}{2}(15.6 + 19.4)(5) = 87.5 \\
35\text{-}40: &\ \tfrac{1}{2}(19.4 + 18.2)(5) = 94.0 \\
40\text{-}50: &\ \tfrac{1}{2}(18.2 + 11.0)(10) = 146.0 \\
50\text{-}60: &\ \tfrac{1}{2}(11.0 + 3.4)(10) = 72.0
\end{aligned}$$
The sum is in $\mathrm{N\,ms}$, so
$$\sum = 21.0 + 70.0 + 127.0 + 87.5 + 94.0 + 146.0 + 72.0 = 617.5\ \mathrm{N\,ms} \;\; (A1).$$
$$J = 617.5 \times 10^{-3} = 0.6175\ \mathrm{N\,s} \approx 0.62\ \mathrm{N\,s} \;\; (A1).$$
The unit is the newton second, $\mathrm{N\,s}$, equivalently $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$.

**(c)** The impulse equals the change in momentum, $J = \Delta p = m(v - u)$ with $u = +0.450\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ (M1):
$$v = u + \frac{J}{m} = 0.450 + \frac{0.6175}{0.850} = 0.450 + 0.7265 = 1.18\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}} \;\; (A1).$$

A candidate who assumes a constant $10\ \mathrm{ms}$ interval weights the two short intervals as though they were twice as long:
$$\sum = 21.0 + 70.0 + 127.0 + 175.0 + 188.0 + 146.0 + 72.0 = 799.0\ \mathrm{N\,ms},$$
so $J = 0.799\ \mathrm{N\,s}$ and $v = 0.450 + \dfrac{0.799}{0.850} = 1.39\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ (A1).

The error is $\dfrac{799.0 - 617.5}{617.5} = 29\%$ in the impulse and $($1.39 - 1.18$)/$1.18$ = 18\%$ in the speed. It arises entirely from the two $5\ \mathrm{ms}$ intervals at the peak, where the force is largest and where doubling the assumed width adds the most area.

**(d)** The sampling interval should have been fixed by the operator and recorded with the data, together with a note of any change; on an automatic rate the interval is a property of the logger rather than of the experiment, and a record whose abscissa is not documented cannot be integrated unambiguously. A second clock channel, or a fixed rate with the interval written in the log, would settle it (A1).

Given the record as it stands, the honest estimate of the uncertainty in the impulse comes from the force resolution: each sample carries $\pm 0.2\ \mathrm{N}$, and the trapezium rule weights each sample by half the sum of the two intervals that touch it, namely $\tfrac{1}{2}(10 + 10) = 10\ \mathrm{ms}$ for an interior sample at a $10\ \mathrm{ms}$ step and $\tfrac{1}{2}(10 + 5) = 7.5\ \mathrm{ms}$ for one at the junction. Adding the contributions in quadrature gives a few tenths of a per cent of the total, so the resolution is not the limiting factor -- the sampling interval is (A1). The duration itself has no quoted uncertainty, so a defensible statement is that the impulse is known to about $1\%$ from the record and to whatever the undocumented interval change contributes on top.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) (A1) for both intervals $10\ \mathrm{ms}$ and $5\ \mathrm{ms}$ located in the right part of the record, (A1) for the reason the actual differences must be used. A candidate who says only "the intervals are not constant" scores the first mark if the two values are named.

(b) (M1) for the trapezium rule applied interval by interval with the correct widths, (A1) for $617.5\ \mathrm{N\,ms}$, (A1) for $0.6175\ \mathrm{N\,s}$ or $0.62\ \mathrm{N\,s}$ with the unit. Working left in $\mathrm{N\,ms}$ and converted at the end is the expected route; a candidate who converts each term to $\mathrm{N\,s}$ first and reaches $0.6175$ scores the same. A candidate who obtains $799\ \mathrm{N\,ms}$ scores the method mark only, and this is the discriminating case for part (c).

(c) (M1) for $J = m\Delta v$ with the correct sign convention and $u = 0.450\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, (A1) for $1.18\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, (A1) for the constant-interval value $0.799\ \mathrm{N\,s}$ and $1.39\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. A candidate who adds the impulse to the initial momentum in the wrong direction -- obtaining $0.450 - 0.7265$ -- forfeits the second mark; the trolley bounces off the sensor and its speed increases, which the data support since the force is always positive.

(d) (A1) for a concrete suggestion about recording the interval, (A1) for an uncertainty estimate that names the resolution and the weights. A candidate who computes a percentage from the resolution alone, without noticing that the interval is the dominant unknown, scores the first mark only.

Condonation: a candidate who writes the answer to (b) as $0.618\ \mathrm{N\,s}$ or $0.62\ \mathrm{N\,s}$ scores full marks; two or three significant figures are both acceptable here, since the forced resolution is $0.2\ \mathrm{N}$. Follow-through: a candidate whose (b) is $799\ \mathrm{N\,ms}$ and who then obtains $1.39\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ in (c) is fully credited the (M1) and (A1) for the method and the arithmetic, and is expected to identify $1.18$ in the second half of (c).

Forfeits: treating the force-time record as a triangle and using $\tfrac{1}{2}F_{\max}t$; taking the sum of the forces as the impulse, which omits the time dimension entirely.
questions.explanation:
This question is about a collision and it is not really about collisions. The physics is one line -- impulse is the area under a force-time graph and equals the change in momentum -- and the work is in noticing what the data actually are.

The record has eight samples and seven intervals, and the intervals are not equal: two of them are $5\ \mathrm{ms}$ where the rest are $10\ \mathrm{ms}$. This is not a hypothetical hazard. Loggers with an automatic rate setting really do change interval mid-record, usually to capture detail where the signal is changing fastest, which is exactly where the force is largest and where the area is most sensitive to the width assumed. The two short intervals carry a total area of $181.5\ \mathrm{N\,ms}$; treating them as $10\ \mathrm{ms}$ each makes that $350\ \mathrm{N\,ms}$, and the impulse comes out $29\%$ too large.

The reason this is a trap worth setting is that nothing about the numbers looks wrong. The forces are plausible and rise and fall smoothly, the times are in increasing order, and the table is not missing any rows. A candidate who reads the force column and takes the step for granted is doing arithmetic on an assumed dataset rather than the one in front of them, and the mark scheme is arranged so that this candidate scores the method mark in (b) and then sees, in (c), exactly what the assumption cost. Showing the wrong value inside the question rather than merely penalising it is deliberate: the point is that $1.39$ and $1.18$ are both "reasonable" numbers for a trolley to rebound with, and only the time column distinguishes them.

Part (d) is where the item finishes rather than where it tails off. The uncertainty in the impulse is *not* dominated by the sensor's resolution -- that contributes a few tenths of a per cent -- but by whether the abscissa can be trusted at all, which is a recording decision made before the collision happened. A candidate who produces a careful quadrature sum from the resolution and reports a comfortable $0.2\%$ has answered a question that the data do not support, and saying so is the judgement this part rewards.

provenance.adaptation: Original. Impulse as the area under a force-time record is a standard practical treatment; the item's construction -- an automatic sampling rate that changes interval exactly at the peak of the collision -- is written here so that the dominant uncertainty is in the record's abscissa rather than in the sensor's resolution.

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Read the force column, see eight samples, take the time step to be ten milliseconds throughout because that is the step between the first several rows, and compute the impulse as the trapezium sum of the forces multiplied by that constant step.
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: The logger's automatic rate changed the interval to five milliseconds for the two samples at the peak of the collision, so the constant-step assumption doubles the width of exactly the intervals that carry the largest forces and inflates the area without any of the numbers looking wrong.
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: The impulse is reported as seven hundred and ninety nine thousandths of a newton second instead of six hundred and eighteen, the speed after the collision comes out at one point three nine metres per second instead of one point one eight, and both numbers are plausible enough to be accepted without a second look.

verification.method: The trapezium sum was evaluated interval by interval from the tabulated pairs and the result converted to SI, then checked against the constant-step sum to quantify the assumption's cost. Momentum conservation was used to convert the impulse into a speed and the arithmetic checked for both the correct and the incorrect step. The sum of the individual trapezium terms was verified against the closed-form sum of all seven contributions.
solution_skeleton: read the time column and separate the intervals of different width
apply the trapezium rule interval by interval with the width actually recorded
convert the accumulated area from newton milliseconds to newton seconds
divide the impulse by the mass to obtain the change in speed and add it to the approach speed
repeat the area with a constant step to quantify what the assumption costs

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.syllabus_ref: Theme D: Fields, D.3 Motion in electromagnetic fields (charged particles in a uniform magnetic field, circular motion, the cyclotron); Theme A: A.3 Work, energy and power (energy gained across a potential difference).
questions.subtopic: D.3 A cyclotron, whose exit energy is fixed by the flux density and the radius of the dees and not by the accelerating potential difference, so that raising the voltage changes the number of revolutions rather than the energy
questions.question: A cyclotron is to be used to accelerate protons, and its operating frequency and exit energy must be established. Show that the time for a proton to complete one full circular path inside the dees is $T = \dfrac{2\pi m}{qB}$ and that this time does not depend on the proton's speed, and calculate the frequency the alternating potential difference must have. Then determine the maximum speed the protons can reach, calculate the maximum kinetic energy and the number of revolutions a proton makes, and explain what does and does not raise the maximum energy.
questions.challenge_mechanism: The alternating potential difference is the only thing that puts energy into the protons, one gap crossing at a time, so it is entirely natural to conclude that the energy the protons leave with is proportional to it. It is not. The protons leave when their path has grown to the radius of the dees, and that condition fixes the exit speed through $v = qBR/m$ and the exit energy through $	frac{1}{2}q^2B^2R^2/m$, both of which are independent of the voltage. Raising the voltage does make each crossing worth more, and it therefore reduces the number of revolutions needed, but the product of those two quantities is held constant by the geometry. The item also asks for the period first, because the reason the machine works at all is that the period is speed-independent, which is what allows one fixed frequency to serve the whole acceleration.

stimulus.title: A cyclotron at a teaching hospital
stimulus.body:
A cyclotron produces a beam of protons that is used to make short-lived radioisotopes for a hospital's scanning service. The protons are injected near the centre of two hollow semicircular electrodes, the *dees*, and are accelerated each time they cross the gap between them by an alternating potential difference applied across that gap. A uniform magnetic flux density $B = 1.2\ \mathrm{T}$ acts at right angles to the plane of the dees, and each dee has a radius $R = 0.35\ \mathrm{m}$. The alternating potential difference has a peak value of $50\ \mathrm{kV}$.

A proton has charge $+e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$ and mass $m = 1.67 \times 10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg}$. Treat the protons as non-relativistic throughout, and take the speed of light as $c = 3.00 \times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the time $T$ taken by a proton to complete one full circular path inside the dees is $T = \dfrac{2\pi m}{qB}$, and that this time is independent of the proton's speed. Calculate $T$ for the fields given, and hence state the frequency at which the alternating potential difference must be applied.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the maximum speed of a proton as it leaves the cyclotron, and express this speed as a fraction of the speed of light.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the maximum kinetic energy of the protons in joules and in MeV, and hence calculate the number of revolutions a proton makes before it leaves the cyclotron.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why raising the peak value of the alternating potential difference does not increase the maximum kinetic energy of the protons, and state one change to the apparatus that would increase it.

questions.answer:
**(a)** Inside a dee the only force is the magnetic force, and it acts at right angles to the velocity, so it supplies the centripetal force (D.3):
$$qvB = \frac{mv^{2}}{r} \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad r = \frac{mv}{qB}.$$
The circumference of the circular path is $2\pi r$, and the proton covers it at speed $v$, so
$$T = \frac{2\pi r}{v} = \frac{2\pi}{v} \cdot \frac{mv}{qB} = \frac{2\pi m}{qB} \;\; (M1)(A1).$$
The speed cancels. That is the whole reason the machine works: a faster proton has a larger radius but covers the larger circumference in the same time, so a single fixed frequency accelerates the proton all the way out (A1).

Numerically,
$$T = \frac{2\pi \times 1.67 \times 10^{-27}}{1.60 \times 10^{-19} \times 1.2} = 5.47 \times 10^{-8}\ \mathrm{s},$$
so the alternating potential difference must be supplied at
$$f = \frac{1}{T} = 1.83 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{Hz} \approx 18\ \mathrm{MHz}.$$
The proton crosses the gap twice in each revolution, so the potential difference must complete one full cycle in the same time $T$; the required frequency is therefore $f = qB/2\pi m$, about $18\ \mathrm{MHz}$.

**(b)** The protons leave when the radius of the path has grown to the radius of the dees, $r = R$ (D.3). From $r = mv/qB$,
$$v_{\max} = \frac{qBR}{m} = \frac{1.60 \times 10^{-19} \times 1.2 \times 0.35}{1.67 \times 10^{-27}} = 4.02 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}} \;\; (M1)(A1).$$
As a fraction of the speed of light this is
$$\frac{v_{\max}}{c} = \frac{4.02 \times 10^{7}}{3.00 \times 10^{8}} = 0.134,$$
about thirteen per cent of $c$. That justifies the non-relativistic treatment, since the mass of a proton at $0.134c$ is only about $0.9\%$ greater than its rest mass.

**(c)** The maximum kinetic energy follows from the speed in part (b):
$$E_{k} = \tfrac{1}{2}mv_{\max}^{2} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 1.67 \times 10^{-27} \times (4.02 \times 10^{7})^{2} = 1.35 \times 10^{-12}\ \mathrm{J} \;\; (A1).$$
Equivalently, and more directly from the geometry,
$$E_{k} = \frac{q^{2}B^{2}R^{2}}{2m} = \frac{(1.60 \times 10^{-19} \times 1.2 \times 0.35)^{2}}{2 \times 1.67 \times 10^{-27}} = 1.35 \times 10^{-12}\ \mathrm{J}.$$
In electronvolts,
$$E_{k} = \frac{1.35 \times 10^{-12}}{1.60 \times 10^{-19}} = 8.4 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{eV} = 8.4\ \mathrm{MeV} \;\; (A1).$$

A proton gains energy $qV$ each time it crosses the gap, and it crosses the gap twice per revolution, so it gains $2qV = 2 \times 1.60 \times 10^{-19} \times 5.0 \times 10^{4} = 1.60 \times 10^{-14}\ \mathrm{J}$ per revolution. The number of revolutions is therefore
$$N = \frac{1.35 \times 10^{-12}}{1.60 \times 10^{-14}} = 84.5,$$
that is about $85$ revolutions (A1). The protons cross the gap about $169$ times. Since the period does not change as the protons speed up, the total acceleration time is simply $N T = 84.5 \times 5.47 \times 10^{-8} \approx 4.6\ \mu\mathrm{s}$.

**(d)** The protons leave when the radius has grown to the fixed radius of the dees, and the speed at that moment is fixed by the fields through $v = qBR/m$ (D.3). Because $R$, $B$, $m$ and $q$ are all properties of the apparatus or the particle, the exit speed is fixed too, and so is the exit energy $\tfrac{1}{2}q^{2}B^{2}R^{2}/m$ (A1).

The voltage never appears in that expression. What the voltage sets is the *energy per crossing*, $qV$, and so the number of crossings needed, $E_{k}/qV$. Raising the voltage from $50\ \mathrm{kV}$ to $100\ \mathrm{kV}$ would double the energy gained at each crossing and halve the number of revolutions, from about $85$ to about $42$, leaving the energy the protons leave with unchanged (A1). The product of the two is the same because both are constrained by the same geometry: the protons have to reach the same radius, and reaching it requires the same total energy however it was delivered.

To raise the maximum energy, the ceiling itself has to be moved. Since $E_{k} = \tfrac{1}{2}q^{2}B^{2}R^{2}/m$, a larger flux density $B$ or a larger dee radius $R$ would do it; both appear squared, so a $10\%$ increase in either raises the maximum energy by about $21\%$ (A1). Increasing $B$ is the cheaper change in practice because it does not require a larger magnet, but it runs into the relativistic limit: once $v$ is an appreciable fraction of $c$, the proton's mass increases and its period $T = 2\pi m/qB$ is no longer constant, so the fixed frequency falls out of step with the protons and the acceleration stalls. A cyclotron can only be extended in $B$ or $R$ until that happens, which is why higher-energy machines use a varying frequency.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) (M1) for equating the magnetic force to the centripetal force, (A1) for cancelling $v$ to obtain $T = 2\pi m/qB$, (A1) for the value $5.47 \times 10^{-8}\ \mathrm{s}$ and the frequency $1.83 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{Hz}$ (accept $18\ \mathrm{MHz}$ or $1.8 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{Hz}$). The independence of the speed must be stated, not merely shown by cancellation; a candidate who derives $T$ but does not draw the conclusion forfeits the third mark.

(b) (M1) for the substitution $r = R$ into $r = mv/qB$, (A1) for $4.02 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ (accept $4.0 \times 10^{7}$). The fraction $0.134$ is not separately marked but is expected as the justification for the non-relativistic treatment; a candidate who used a relativistic mass without being asked does not lose marks, provided the value is consistent.

(c) (A1) for $1.35 \times 10^{-12}\ \mathrm{J}$ (accept $1.4 \times 10^{-12}$), (A1) for $8.4\ \mathrm{MeV}$, (A1) for $84.5$ or about $85$ revolutions. A candidate who obtains the energy by multiplying $qV$ by a *fixed* number of crossings has made the central error of the item and will not match the energy; if by luck they do match, the third mark is still forfeited because the reasoning is wrong.

(d) (A1) for stating that the exit speed and therefore the energy are fixed by $B$, $R$ and the particle's $q/m$. (A1) for explaining that the voltage controls the energy per crossing and hence the number of revolutions, with the product unchanged. (A1) for naming a change to the apparatus that raises the ceiling, correctly to $B$ or $R$ (not the voltage). A candidate who says only "increase the voltage" scores at most the first mark.

Forfeits: using $r = m v / q B$ with the wrong mass, such as the electron mass; treating $T$ as depending on $v$; using $E_k = qV$ with $V = 50\ \mathrm{kV}$, which gives $8.0 \times 10^{-15}\ \mathrm{J}$ and is three orders of magnitude out; giving the frequency as $2 \times 18\ \mathrm{MHz}$ on the argument that the proton crosses the gap twice per revolution, which confuses crossings with cycles. Condonation: energies quoted as $8.4$ or $8.45\ \mathrm{MeV}$ are both accepted; the number of revolutions may be given as $84$, $84.5$ or $85$ provided the method is shown, since the proton leaves part-way through its final revolution.
questions.explanation:
The interesting thing about a cyclotron is not the force arithmetic, which is two lines long, but the fact that the machine works at all. A proton that is moving faster should take longer to go round a bigger circle; the reason it does not is that the radius and the speed grow together, so the period is unchanged. Every cyclotron question that is worth asking is a consequence of that cancellation, and this item asks for it first because the rest of the question only makes sense once it is understood.

Part (a) is the derivation. From $qvB = mv^2/r$ the radius is $mv/qB$, the circumference is proportional to $v$, and the time to cover it does not depend on $v$ at all. That is what allows a single fixed-frequency supply to serve the whole acceleration: the protons come round in step with the voltage no matter how fast they are going. A student who has memorised $T = 2\pi m/qB$ can quote it; the part asks for the cancellation explicitly.

Part (c) is where the difficulty sits. The tempting route is to say that a proton gains $qV$ per crossing and therefore ends up with $qV$ times the number of crossings, and then to invent a number of crossings from the observation that the protons leave after roughly eighty-five turns. That reasoning is circular and gets the answer right only by accident. The honest route is to note that the protons leave when $r = R$, which fixes $v$, which fixes the energy, and then to work out the number of revolutions as a consequence. The two routes give the same number, which is exactly why the error survives: the answer is right and the mechanism is wrong.

Part (d) is the part that separates the two. The voltage is the only thing putting energy in, and yet it cannot change what the protons leave with. What it changes is how many bites at the apple are needed. Doubling the voltage halves the number of revolutions and leaves the exit energy alone. The exit energy is a property of the apparatus -- the magnet and the size of the dees -- and to change it one of those has to change. This is a genuinely useful thing to know about particle accelerators, and it is the reason that the largest cyclotrons were abandoned in favour of machines that vary the frequency or the field.

provenance.adaptation: Original. The cyclotron is standard D.3 material, but published treatments usually ask for the resonance frequency and the exit speed and stop; this item adds the energy ceiling, the count of revolutions, and the explanation of why the accelerating voltage does not appear in the expression for the exit energy, which is the part students most often get wrong.

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Treat the energy delivered by the potential difference as the thing that decides the exit energy, and reason that a proton gaining qV at each of roughly eighty-five revolutions must leave with eighty-five times qV, so that a larger voltage would give the protons more energy.
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: The exit energy is not set by the voltage but by the condition that the path has grown to the fixed radius of the dees, which fixes the speed through v = qBR/m and the energy through half q squared B squared R squared over m; the number of revolutions is itself equal to the energy divided by the energy per crossing, so raising the voltage lowers the count and leaves their product where it was.
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: The maximum kinetic energy is reported as the voltage times the charge times a fixed number of crossings -- for instance 85 times 2qV as separate crossings -- and the conclusion is drawn that increasing the peak voltage from 50 kV to 100 kV would double the exit energy, when it would in fact halve the number of revolutions and change the energy not at all.

verification.method: The period, frequency, exit speed and exit energy were computed from the stated charge, mass, flux density and radius, and the exit energy was obtained twice, once as half m v squared from the speed and once in closed form as q squared B squared R squared over 2m, the two agreeing to four significant figures. The number of revolutions was found by dividing the exit energy by 2qV and the result checked against the count of gap crossings in the answer text. The relativistic correction at the exit speed was computed as the fractional increase in mass at v = 0.134c and used to justify the non-relativistic treatment in the stimulus.
solution_skeleton: equate the magnetic force to the centripetal force and cancel the speed to obtain the period
invert the period to obtain the fixed frequency the alternating supply must have
apply the condition that the radius has grown to the radius of the dees to obtain the exit speed
square the exit speed to obtain the maximum kinetic energy and divide by the energy per crossing
identify which quantities fix the exit energy and which only fix how quickly it is reached

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.syllabus_ref: E.4 Fission, with E.3 Radioactive decay and B.1 Thermal energy transfers
questions.topic: Theme E: Nuclear and quantum physics
questions.subtopic: E.4 The fuel-cycle arithmetic of a fission reactor carried through from the energy per fission to the mass of enriched uranium per year, and the sensitivity of the comparison with coal to the assumptions behind it
questions.challenge_mechanism: The arithmetic is a chain of five conversions and the trap is at the fourth: the mass of uranium that has fissioned is not the mass of fuel loaded, because natural uranium is not fissile and the fuel is enriched to a stated fraction of $^{235}\mathrm{U}$. A candidate who stops at $377\ \mathrm{kg}$ has answered the question that was asked one part earlier. The evaluation then turns on the assumptions rather than the numbers -- the $4\%$ figure is the $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ fraction of the fuel, and the comparison with coal ignores the mining, enrichment and waste handling, all of which are energy costs the fission chain does not incur in the same way.
questions.question: A pressurised water reactor operates with a thermal power output of $3.0\ \mathrm{GW}$ and converts this to electrical energy with an efficiency of $33\%$. Each fission of a $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ nucleus releases $202\ \mathrm{MeV}$. The reactor is refuelled with uranium enriched to $4.0\%$ $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ by mass, and the remainder is $^{238}\mathrm{U}$, which does not undergo fission in this reactor. Use $N_{A} = 6.02 \times 10^{23}\ \mathrm{mol^{-1}}$, $1\ \mathrm{eV} = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}$ and one year $= 3.15 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{s}$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the fission of all the nuclei in $1.00\ \mathrm{kg}$ of $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ would release about $8.3 \times 10^{13}\ \mathrm{J}$ of energy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the mass of $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ that undergoes fission in one year of continuous operation at the stated output.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine the mass of enriched uranium that must be loaded each year to supply that quantity of $^{235}\mathrm{U}$, and determine the mass of coal that would be needed each year to generate the same electrical energy in a station burning coal of energy content $2.4 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$ at an efficiency of $38\%$.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Evaluate the comparison in part (c) as a measure of the environmental advantage of the reactor, referring to at least two assumptions that the comparison makes.

questions.answer:
**(a)** The number of $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ nuclei in $1.00\ \mathrm{kg}$ (M1):
$$N = \frac{1.00}{235 \times 10^{-3}}\ \mathrm{mol} \times 6.02 \times 10^{23}\ \mathrm{mol^{-1}} = \frac{1000}{235} \times 6.02 \times 10^{23} = 2.56 \times 10^{24}.$$

The energy released per fission is
$$202\ \mathrm{MeV} = 202 \times 10^{6} \times 1.60 \times 10^{-19} = 3.23 \times 10^{-11}\ \mathrm{J},$$
so
$$E = 2.56 \times 10^{24} \times 3.23 \times 10^{-11} = 8.28 \times 10^{13}\ \mathrm{J} \approx 8.3 \times 10^{13}\ \mathrm{J} \;\; (A1).$$

**(b)** The electrical output is
$$P_{e} = 0.33 \times 3.0 \times 10^{9} = 9.9 \times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{W} \;\; (M1).$$
In one year the electrical energy delivered is
$$E_{e} = 9.9 \times 10^{8} \times 3.15 \times 10^{7} = 3.12 \times 10^{16}\ \mathrm{J} \;\; (M1).$$
All of this comes from fission, so the mass of $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ fissioned is
$$m = \frac{3.12 \times 10^{16}}{8.28 \times 10^{13}} = 377\ \mathrm{kg} \;\; (A1).$$

It is worth noting that the efficiency cancels out of nothing here: the thermal power of $3.0\ \mathrm{GW}$ is what the fuel must supply, so an alternative route is to use $3.0 \times 10^{9}\ \mathrm{W}$ directly and compute $m = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{9} \times 3.15 \times 10^{7}}{8.28 \times 10^{13}} = 1141\ \mathrm{kg}$ of $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ -- but that is the mass fissioned to supply the *thermal* output, and the electrical output is what the question asks about. Working in electrical energy throughout, as above, avoids the confusion.

**(c)** The $377\ \mathrm{kg}$ is $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ alone. Since the fuel contains only $4.0\%$ $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ by mass (M1):
$$m_{\text{fuel}} = \frac{377}{0.040} = 9.4 \times 10^{3}\ \mathrm{kg} \approx 9.4\ \mathrm{tonnes} \;\; (A1).$$
So just under ten tonnes of enriched uranium per year, of which about $9.0\ \mathrm{t}$ is $^{238}\mathrm{U}$ that does not fission.

For coal, the energy must be supplied as chemical energy and the conversion is less efficient:
$$m_{\text{coal}} = \frac{3.12 \times 10^{16}}{0.38 \times 2.4 \times 10^{7}} = 3.4 \times 10^{9}\ \mathrm{kg} = 3.4 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{tonnes} \;\; (A1).$$

The ratio of the two masses is $\dfrac{3.4 \times 10^{9}}{9.4 \times 10^{3}} \approx 3.6 \times 10^{5}$: the coal station consumes about three hundred and sixty thousand times the mass of fuel, each year.

**(d)** The comparison is a ratio of two masses and it is a real effect -- five and a half orders of magnitude is not a rounding difference -- but it is not a measure of environmental impact, and the assumptions that break the identification are worth naming.

First, the comparison counts only the fuel delivered to the station. It ignores everything upstream of that point, and the two chains are not alike. The coal figure of $3.4 \times 10^{6}$ tonnes is coal that has been mined, washed and transported, and those steps consume energy and produce emissions of their own; but the nuclear figure of $9.4$ tonnes is *enriched* uranium, and enrichment is an energy-intensive process that consumes electricity, historically generated by burning fossil fuel. A fair comparison adds the enrichment energy and the mining and milling energy to the nuclear side, and adds the transport energy to the coal side, before comparing (A1).

Second, the comparison assumes the two stations are otherwise equivalent in what they produce, and they are not. The coal station's $3.4$ million tonnes leave the plant every year as $\mathrm{CO_{2}}$ -- roughly $9 \times 10^{6}$ tonnes of it, since each tonne of coal of this energy content gives about $2.6$ tonnes of $\mathrm{CO_{2}}$ -- which is the environmental advantage the comparison is meant to capture, and it is a genuine one. But the nuclear station produces about $9.4$ tonnes of spent fuel per year which is intensely radioactive for decades and must be stored and eventually disposed of, and the comparison assigns that waste a mass of zero (A1).

Third, the numbers themselves are conditional. The $202\ \mathrm{MeV}$ per fission and the $4.0\%$ enrichment are both stated, and both could be different; more importantly the comparison assumes continuous operation at full output for a whole year, whereas a real reactor is shut for refuelling and maintenance and runs at part load at other times, so the $377\ \mathrm{kg}$ is a lower bound on the $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ consumed per year for a station of this rating. A station with a load factor of $80\%$ would consume about $80\%$ of the fuel but also generate $80\%$ of the energy, so the ratio in (c) is unchanged -- which is worth pointing out, because it shows the ratio is robust to that particular assumption even though the absolute masses are not (A1).
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) (M1) for the number of nuclei from the molar mass and Avogadro's constant, (A1) for the energy, quoted as $8.3 \times 10^{13}\ \mathrm{J}$ or $8.28 \times 10^{13}\ \mathrm{J}$. A candidate who uses $235\ \mathrm{u}$ converted to kilograms ($3.90 \times 10^{-25}\ \mathrm{kg}$) reaches the same answer by dividing rather than by using the mole, and scores full marks.

(b) (M1) for the electrical power, (M1) for the energy in one year, (A1) for $377\ \mathrm{kg}$. A candidate who obtains $1141\ \mathrm{kg}$ by using the thermal power has misread which output the question asks about and scores the first method mark and nothing else; the phrase "same electrical energy" in (c) settles it. Accept values in the range $3.7$ to $3.8 \times 10^{2}\ \mathrm{kg}$.

(c) (M1) for dividing by the enrichment fraction, (A1) for $9.4 \times 10^{3}\ \mathrm{kg}$; (A1) for the coal mass $3.4 \times 10^{9}\ \mathrm{kg}$. The coal calculation can use either the electrical energy (dividing by $0.38$ as well) or the thermal energy; a candidate who uses the electrical energy without dividing by the lower efficiency obtains $1.3 \times 10^{9}\ \mathrm{kg}$ and forfeits the third mark, because the whole point of the comparison is that the coal station wastes more of its input. Follow-through from (b) is allowed.

(d) (A1) for a first assumption stated and used, (A1) for a second, (A1) for the reasoning that connects the assumption to the conclusion -- that is, a candidate must say not only what the comparison ignores but whether ignoring it strengthens or weakens the claimed advantage. Naming the waste as an unaccounted cost scores the mark; listing "waste" and "emissions" and stopping does not.

Forfeits: treating the $4.0\%$ as the fraction of the uranium that fissions rather than as the fraction of the fuel that is $^{235}\mathrm{U}$; using $238$ in the molar mass because "most of the fuel is $^{238}\mathrm{U}$", which confuses the mass loaded with the mass fissioned. Condonations: answers quoted in tonnes or in kilograms are both accepted, and the ratio in (c) may be given as an order of magnitude ($\sim 10^{5}$).
questions.explanation:
This item is a chain of unit conversions and it is set because chains of unit conversions are where the interesting mistakes live. There are five steps: energy per fission in joules, nuclei per kilogram, energy per kilogram, energy per year at the stated output, mass per year. Every one of them is straightforward and the total is forty seconds of arithmetic for a candidate who knows what they are converting.

The mistake the item is built around is a substitution at the fourth step. The mass that fissions is $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ and it is $377\ \mathrm{kg}$. The mass that is *loaded* is fuel, and the fuel is $4.0\%$ $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ because natural uranium is only $0.7\%$ fissile and a reactor cannot run on that. So the loaded mass is twenty-five times the fissioned mass. A candidate who reports $377\ \mathrm{kg}$ as the annual fuel requirement has done every calculation correctly and answered a different question, and the numbers are arranged so that $377$ is a perfectly plausible-looking answer to the question that was actually asked one part earlier.

The second thing to notice is the direction of the efficiency correction. The reactor's $33\%$ efficiency means two thirds of the fission energy leaves as heat that is discarded, so the fuel requirement is set by the electrical output divided by the efficiency -- or, equivalently, by the thermal output directly. The coal station's $38\%$ efficiency works the same way and in the same direction, and a candidate who forgets it on one side of the comparison but not the other produces a ratio that is wrong by a factor of about $1.15$ for no reason at all.

Part (d) is deliberately open and the mark scheme says what it wants: two assumptions, each connected to whether it strengthens or weakens the claimed advantage. The strongest answer is the one that separates the two things the ratio measures. As a statement about *fuel mass* the comparison is excellent and robust -- five and a half orders of magnitude survive any plausible correction, including the enrichment energy, which is large but not a millionth of the coal chain. As a statement about *environmental impact* the ratio is much weaker, because the two waste streams are different in kind and not merely in mass: a coal station's annual output is millions of tonnes of carbon dioxide dispersed into the atmosphere, and a nuclear station's is ten tonnes of spent fuel which is dangerous for decades and must be stored. Neither the mass of the coal nor the mass of the fuel captures that, and the honest answer says so.

provenance.adaptation: Adapted from the standard A-level treatment of nuclear fuel-cycle arithmetic. The rewrite keeps the energy-per-fission conversion but restructures the arc so that the enrichment step is the discriminating part, and replaces the usual single evaluation sentence with a part that requires two named assumptions to be connected to their effect on the conclusion.
provenance.resource_origin: A-level Physics nuclear fuel cycle and power station efficiency calculations

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Carry the energy conversion chain through from the energy per fission to the mass of uranium consumed in a year and report that mass as the annual fuel requirement, because every step of the chain is a conversion the candidate has performed before and the last number obtained is the answer.
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: The mass consumed and the mass loaded are different quantities, because the fuel is enriched to four per cent of the fissile isotope by mass while the arithmetic of the chain up to that point has tracked only the isotope that actually fissions, so the loaded mass is twenty five times the number the chain produces.
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: The annual fuel requirement is reported as about three hundred and eighty kilograms of uranium, and the comparison with coal is then made against that mass, which understates the fuel actually loaded and overstates the mass advantage by a factor of twenty five.

verification.method: Every conversion in the chain was recomputed from first principles with the stated constants, and the energy per kilogram was cross-checked by the independent route of converting 235 u to kilograms and dividing. The annual masses were then recomputed for both the thermal and the electrical output to make sure the two routes through the efficiency agree. The carbon dioxide figure quoted in the evaluation was derived from the coal mass and its carbon content, and the load-factor argument in the last paragraph of the answer was checked to confirm the ratio is invariant to it.
solution_skeleton: convert the energy released per fission from mega electronvolts to joules
obtain the number of fissile nuclei per kilogram from the molar mass and Avogadro's constant
multiply the energy in one year of electrical output by the reciprocal of the reactor efficiency
divide the mass that fissions by the enrichment fraction to obtain the mass of fuel loaded
apply the coal station's own efficiency to obtain its fuel mass and compare the two on the same basis
